issues.legal_issue: A landlord proves subletting when the evidence establishes that a third party was given possession of part of the rented premises and supports an inference that the possession was for consideration, and the tenant fails to substantiate the explanation that the third party was an employee.
material_facts: The eviction suit alleged that the tenant had allowed a third party to use part of the shop for watch repairs and was receiving daily payment from him.
The tenant admitted the third party’s presence and said he worked in the shop as an employee, but produced no salary or attendance records or other evidence supporting that claim.

The trial court found that the third party had partial possession, was carrying on repair work in the shop, and was paying consideration to the tenant; the landlord’s witness also supported the allegation of payment.
issues.conclusion: Subletting was proved. The High Court erred in finding that the landlord had not pleaded or proved parting with possession, and the trial court’s eviction decision on that ground was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 20(2)(e) and 25 of the U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, subletting requires the tenant to part with possession of the whole or part of the premises in favour of a third party for consideration. The landlord bears the initial burden of proving exclusive possession and consideration; proof of parting with possession may shift the evidential burden to the tenant to explain the third party’s presence. Since such arrangements are often clandestine, consideration may be inferred from the proved facts rather than established by direct evidence. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh, Jagdish Prasad v. Smt. Angoori Devi, Dipak Banerjee v. Lilabati Chakraborty, Smt. Rajbir Kaur v. M/s S. Chokesiri and Co., Kala v. Madho Parshad Vaidya, Joginder Singh Sodhi v. Amar Kaur, Mahendra Saree Emporium (II) v. G.V. Srinivasa Murthy, Bharat Sales Ltd. v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, and Krishnawati v. Hans Raj. It also relied on Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, in explaining the right to enjoy property that a sublease transfers.

rule.if: tenant_eviction_suit_based_on_subletting and landlord_proved_third_party_partial_possession and third_party_used_part_of_premises_for_own_business and evidence_supported_payment_for_possession and tenant_failed_to_substantiate_employment_explanation

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit_based_on_subletting: The proceeding seeks a tenant’s eviction on the ground that the tenant sublet all or part of the rented premises.
predicates.landlord_proved_third_party_partial_poss: The landlord’s evidence establishes that a third party was given possession of part of the rented premises.
predicates.third_party_used_part_of_premises_for_ow: The third party used the premises to carry on a business of his or her own.
predicates.evidence_supported_payment_for_possessio: The evidence supports an inference that the third party’s possession was for payment or other consideration.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_substantiate_employment: The tenant claimed that the third party was an employee but failed to produce evidence that would substantiate that claim.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding based on subletting includes proof of a third party’s possession and own business, evidence supporting payment for that possession, and an unsupported claim that the third party was an employee, the result is that subletting is proved.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court should not displace a trial court’s fact finding merely because it would reach a different conclusion when the finding rests on relevant evidence and the trial court has not relied on irrelevant matters or ignored relevant ones.
material_facts: The trial court considered the pleadings and evidence and found that the third party had partial possession and was not proved to be an employee.
The High Court, in revision, set aside the trial court’s decision on the basis that the necessary pleading and a finding of exclusive possession were missing.

The Supreme Court found that the pleading alleged use of part of the shop for the third party’s business in return for payment, that evidence supported parting with possession, and that the trial court had not considered irrelevant matters or ignored relevant evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s interference with the trial court’s finding was not justified, and its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887 empowers a revisional court to ensure that the decision was given according to law and that there was no miscarriage of justice; its jurisdiction is wider than the jurisdiction under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. It does not, however, make revision equivalent to an appeal. A fact finding may be interfered with where it rests on irrelevant factors or relevant facts have been ignored, but a revisional court should not interfere merely because it might have reached a different conclusion. The Court relied on Hari Shankar v. Rao Girdhari Lal Chowdhury and Mundri Lal v. Sushila Rani.

rule.if: revision_from_small_causes_decision and trial_finding_based_on_relevant_evidence and trial_court_considered_relevant_factors and revisional_interference_rest_on_misreading_of_record

predicates.revision_from_small_causes_decision: The proceeding is a revision from a decision of a small causes court.
predicates.trial_finding_based_on_relevant_evidence: The trial court’s finding of fact is supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.trial_court_considered_relevant_factors: The trial court did not base its finding on irrelevant matters or ignore relevant matters.
predicates.revisional_interference_rest_on_misreadi: The revisional court displaced the finding on a basis contradicted by the pleadings or evidence in the record.

issues.definition: When a revision from a small causes decision challenges a relevant-evidence-based trial finding, and the trial court considered relevant factors while the revisional court relied on a misreading of the record, revisional interference is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant facing eviction may be allowed time to vacate when the tenant requests that accommodation and undertakes to comply with the condition imposed by the court.
material_facts: The respondents remained in possession of the shop and requested time to vacate, stating that they had carried on business there for a long time.
The Court allowed them to remain in possession for a limited period on condition that they file an undertaking before the trial court.
issues.conclusion: The respondents were allowed to remain in possession for one year from the judgment, conditional on filing the required undertaking within four weeks.
issues.legal_principle: The Court granted the respondents’ request for time to vacate on the condition that they provide an undertaking to the trial court; no separate statutory test or earlier case was stated for this discretionary relief.

predicates.eviction_appeal_allowed: The appeal results in an order requiring the occupants to give up possession.
predicates.occupants_requested_time_to_vacate: The occupants asked the court for additional time before giving up possession.
predicates.occupants_undertook_to_comply_with_vacat: The occupants agreed to provide the court-required undertaking concerning their departure.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal results in an order to surrender possession, the occupants request time, and they agree to the required undertaking, temporary possession is allowed.
